nature-econ-546.title: The multiplier effect: how spending snowballs
nature-econ-546.text:
A small fall in consumption or investment can be magnified into declines across the whole economy. Keynes explained how, and the multiplier effect is the name for it: when spending changes national income by a multiple of the initial change. The mechanism is a chain. Initial spending raises income and so consumption, which raises income further, until national income has risen by a multiple. How big depends on {{ref:nature-econ-872}}.

The fiscal multiplier is the ratio of the change in national income to a change in government spending. Richard Kahn proposed the multiplier in 1930 to give rigorous justification for public works. Government spending also generates new tax revenue, so net expenditure is less than the amount spent. Governments use it in recessions, when labor is unemployed and resources idle, to close an output gap.

Multipliers below one have been measured in some cases, such as sports stadiums, suggesting crowding out of private spending. In 2008 testimony, Zandi estimated one-year multipliers of 1.73 for temporary food stamp increases and 0.27 for accelerated depreciation.

nature-econ-877.title: Traffic congestion: the commons on wheels
nature-econ-877.text: Congestion sets in when traffic demands more space than street capacity provides, a point called saturation. Speeds fall, trips lengthen and queues grow. It can be seen as a {{ref:nature-econ-606}}: roads are usually free at the point of use, so drivers have little incentive to hold back until demand is limited by opportunity cost. Adding road capacity tends to attract more traffic, called induced demand. Braess's paradox shows that extra capacity can worsen congestion even without more demand.

nature-econ-875.title: Kin selection: helping relatives at a cost
nature-econ-875.text:
Natural selection can favor a trait that costs the organism but helps its relatives. This is kin selection, and it can lead to altruistic behaviour. It is tied to inclusive fitness, which counts offspring produced and those an individual helps produce, weighted by relatedness. Hamilton's 1964 rule says a behaviour spreads when relatedness times the benefit to the recipient exceeds the cost to the actor.

Altruism can be favoured by kin recognition, or in 'viscous' populations with limited dispersal, where neighbours are usually relatives. Humans favour kin, for example in wills in proportion to relatedness, though many evolutionary psychologists warn that relatedness is not the same as shared genes. Critics such as Alonso and Wilson, and Nowak and Tarnita, dispute inclusive fitness theory.

nature-econ-874.title: Common knowledge: knowing that everyone knows
nature-econ-874.text: Common knowledge is knowledge shared by a group such that everyone knows it, everyone knows that everyone knows it, and so on without end. David Lewis introduced the idea in philosophy in his 1969 study Convention, and Robert Aumann gave it a set-theoretic form in 1976. A trustworthy public announcement makes a fact common knowledge, but telling each agent privately yields only mutual knowledge. The blue-eyed islanders puzzle shows its force: after a public announcement that at least one has blue eyes, all k blue-eyed people leave on the kth dawn.

nature-econ-673.title: Reserve price: the seller's floor
nature-econ-673.text: A seller who fears a giveaway sets a reserve price, a minimum below which the auctioned item will not be sold. It can be announced to bidders or kept secret. The reserve protects the seller from a low bid but may lower the final price if it dampens interest. A no-reserve, or absolute, auction sells the item whatever the price, which can draw more bidders hoping for a bargain. Riley and Samuelson showed that discriminating against low-value buyers with a minimum price raises expected revenue.

nature-econ-876.title: Population cycles: boom and bust in the wild
nature-econ-876.text: Snowshoe hare catches in Hudson's Bay Company records ran in a cycle of about ten years. That is a population cycle: a population that rises and falls over a predictable period. Predators track prey. More prey means more food for predators, and when prey declines, predator numbers come under pressure. Food supply, disease and climate all influence population change too, yet the full cause of cycles is a major unsolved ecological problem.

nature-econ-077.title: Reciprocity: kindness for kindness
nature-econ-077.text: Answer a kind act with kindness and an unfair one with unkindness, and you are driven by reciprocity. In social psychology it is a learned norm of answering an action with an equivalent one, rewarding positive actions and punishing negative ones. Positive reciprocity returns a favour with one of roughly equal positive value. Fehr and Gächter's public goods experiments showed people in reciprocal settings deviate from pure self-interest more than in other contexts. Reciprocity often exceeds what rational self-interest predicts and tends to win out over it in competitive markets with incomplete contracts.

nature-econ-674.title: The winner's curse: when winning means overpaying
nature-econ-674.text: The bidder who wins an auction may be the one who most overvalued the prize. The winner's curse is the tendency of a winner who knows less about an item than the seller to overvalue it and overpay. It arises in common-value settings, where actual values are unknown but correlated and bidders bid on estimates. When items go to whoever overvalues them most, resources may not end up with the person who values them most. Bid shading, bidding below one's true value, guards against the curse. It risks losing the auction but may win the item cheaply.

nature-econ-867.title: The Malthusian growth model: growth in proportion to size
nature-econ-867.text:
In 1798 Thomas Malthus wrote his Essay on the Principle of Population, and one of the simplest models in biology bears his name. In the Malthusian growth model, a population's growth is proportional to its current size. It is often called the exponential or Malthusian law, and builds on {{ref:nature-econ-442}}. Its parameters are the initial population P0 and the growth rate r, which Fisher called the Malthusian parameter and Lotka the intrinsic rate of increase. Population ecology treats it as the first principle of population dynamics, by analogy with Newton's first law of motion.

Malthus held that life tends to grow exponentially when resources are abundant, but actual growth is limited by available resources. Verhulst, after reading the essay, developed a population model bounded by resource limits in 1838 and named it the logistic function.

nature-econ-854.title: Exogenous and endogenous variables: what the model decides
nature-econ-854.text:
Some values a model takes as given, and others it works out. In an economic model, an exogenous variable has its value set outside the model, while an endogenous variable's value is determined by the model. A variable can be exogenous in one model and endogenous in another, for example when one model is a component of a broader model. The IS model treats the interest rate as exogenous and output as endogenous. The LM model takes income as given and determines the interest rate. Combined in IS-LM, both are endogenous.

Comparative statics compares outcomes before and after a change in an exogenous parameter, using derivatives to see how each endogenous variable moves. In econometrics, an endogenous random variable is correlated with the error term, while an exogenous one is not. This is related to, but distinct from, the modelling sense; see {{ref:nature-econ-223}}.

nature-eco-675.title: Nitrous oxide: the third greenhouse gas
nature-eco-675.text:
Per molecule over 100 years, nitrous oxide traps 265 times as much heat as CO2. Its concentration is under one thousandth of CO2's, so its greenhouse contribution is less than one third that of carbon dioxide. It is a minor atmospheric gas that is an active part of the planetary nitrogen cycle and a long-lived greenhouse gas. It is the third most important greenhouse gas for global warming and has been a major ozone-depleting substance.

Atmospheric abundance has grown more than 20% from about 270 ppb in 1750, surpassing 330 ppb in 2017, and is rising about 1 ppb per year. About 40% of emissions are human-caused, with growth chiefly from expanding agriculture. Annual human emissions equal about 3 billion tonnes of CO2 in greenhouse effect. Microbes produce it by nitrification, denitrification and nitrifier denitrification.

nature-eco-674.title: Ecoregions: mapping nature's distinct communities
nature-eco-674.text:
The WWF first set out 867 terrestrial ecoregions in 14 biomes and 8 biogeographic realms. An ecoregion is a large land or water area defined by its environmental resources, with a geographically distinct assemblage of natural communities and species. WWF's definition requires that communities share most of their species and dynamics, share similar environmental conditions, and interact ecologically in ways critical to their long-term persistence.

Boundaries rarely form abrupt edges. They are bounded by ecotones and mosaic habitats, and most ecoregions contain habitats that differ from their assigned biome. Two systems compete. Bailey's algorithmic system gives priority to climate and ecological criteria, while the WWF system, built for biodiversity conservation planning, gives priority to the distribution of species assemblages.

A 2017 update with satellite imagery reduced the terrestrial count to 846 and later 844. Marine ecoregions number 232, grouped into 62 provinces and 12 realms, and the freshwater map of 2008 has 426 ecoregions. The Global 200 is WWF's list of priority ecoregions for conservation.

nature-eco-671.title: Symbiosis: six ways species live together
nature-eco-671.text: A remora riding a manatee gains, while the manatee neither gains nor loses. That is commensalism, one of six types of symbiosis, the close, long-term interaction between species. The six are mutualism, commensalism, parasitism, neutralism, amensalism and competition, distinguished by the benefit or harm each partner receives. Amensalism harms one organism with no effect on the other, for example antibiotic production by microbes or hoofed mammals trampling grass. The term was long debated over whether it should denote only mutualism, which produced two classifications of interactions: by duration, and by strength of effect.

nature-eco-672.title: Non-trophic interactions: relationships beyond eating
nature-eco-672.text: Not every link between species is a meal. Non-trophic interactions are those that are not feeding relationships, such as habitat modification, mutualism and competition for space. They can indirectly change food web topology and trophic dynamics by affecting the species in the network and the strength of trophic links. Researchers argue that trophic and non-trophic interactions should be integrated in ecological network analysis. The few empirical studies cover a limited number of coastal systems, so it is unclear how far the findings generalize.

nature-eco-670.title: Coevolution: species shaping each other
nature-eco-670.text:
Flowering plants and insects have coevolved for over 100 million years, and the earliest bees appeared in the early Cretaceous. Coevolution is two or more species reciprocally shaping each other's evolution through natural selection. Hummingbirds and bird-pollinated flowers show it as a mutualism: nectar, colour, shape and blooming time match the birds' diet, vision, bills and breeding season.

Hosts and parasites enter an arms race. The Red Queen hypothesis predicts that sexual reproduction lets a host stay just ahead of its parasite. Predators and prey, and herbivores and plants, impose mutual selective pressures that produce arms races and anti-predator adaptations. Coevolution can be pairwise or diffuse among a guild of species, and under the geographic mosaic theory it differs between populations depending on location and community ecology.

Humans induce it too. Disease-resistant crop varieties bred since the 1940s favored rapid evolution in pathogens that overcame the plant defences. Norgaard and Gowdy applied it to economics and society, arguing that the economy, society and the environment are linked in a coevolutionary relationship.

nature-eco-288.title: Top-down and bottom-up control of ecosystems
nature-eco-288.text:
Is an ecosystem built from below or ruled from above? Both. Trophic dynamics is the transfer of energy and nutrients between organisms. Energy captured by plants passes to herbivores, then carnivores, then top carnivores, and the total shrinks at each higher level. Bottom-up control comes from how much energy plants bring in, top-down control from predators. Correlations in abundance or biomass between consumers and resources are the evidence for bottom-up control, as when herbivore and detritivore biomass rises with primary productivity.

Top carnivores keep herbivores in check; without them herbivores could multiply and eat all the plants. If plant populations fall sharply, herbivores decline and then carnivores decline too. An ecosystem need not be one or the other: a marine system may be bottom-up, then come under top-down control during fishing. Predators can dramatically shift which species dominate on land and at sea, and the balance of the two controls is a major research question. Herbivory can also speed litter decomposition and nutrient cycling.

nature-eco-677.title: Three ways to draw a food web
nature-eco-677.text: A food web can be drawn as a bare map, a ledger or a web of influence. Topological webs are non-quantitative maps of which organisms eat which, compared by chain length and connectivity. Flow webs add quantitative carbon or nutrient transfer, built from the biomass of each functional group, usually in kg carbon per hectare, assuming each group is in equilibrium. Interaction webs show how one group influences another, including indirect effects, such as a predator of root herbivores benefiting the plant roots. Community matrix models describe each link with Lotka-Volterra equations plus biomass and feeding data, and can show how small changes affect web stability.
